origin: State Street (runs north-south, divides East from West) and Madison Street (runs east-west, divides North from South)
units_per_mile: 800 address units = 1 mile in the standard system (i.e., 8 blocks per mile, ~100 numbers per standard block). Note: this is the *standard* rate adopted citywide by ordinance; a few older near-Loop south-side streets (Roosevelt Rd, Cermak Rd, 31st St) deviate from it — see caveats.
how_it_works:
Every address in Chicago is really a coordinate pair, even though only one number appears in the street address:
1. Find State & Madison downtown — that's (0,0).
2. Going along any EAST-WEST street (like Addison, Madison, Roosevelt), the number tells you how far EAST or WEST of State Street you are. "1060 W Addison" means 1060 units (≈1.3 mi) west of State St.
3. Going along any NORTH-SOUTH street (like Michigan Ave, Halsted, Wacker), the number tells you how far NORTH or SOUTH of Madison Street you are. "875 N Michigan Ave" means 875 units (≈1.1 mi) north of Madison St.
4. Because the rate is 800 per mile, dividing an address number by 800 gives you the approximate distance in miles from downtown in that direction — e.g., 3600 N ≈ 4.5 miles north of Madison.
5. Practical trick for a visitor: to find where a numbered N-S street (e.g., "3600 N") crosses a named E-W street, or vice versa, remember key mile markers — every major arterial roughly 800 apart is a mile from the last (Madison=0, North Ave=1600N, Fullerton=2400N, Belmont=3200N, Addison=3600N, Irving Park=4000N going north; Roosevelt=1200S, Cermak=2200S, 31st=3100S, 47th=4700S going south; Halsted=800W, Ashland=1600W, Western=2400W, Kedzie=3200W going west; Michigan Ave=100E going east toward the lake).
6. So an address like "1060 W Addison St" effectively encodes the full grid coordinate (3600 N, 1060 W) once you know Addison's own north-south position — which itself is defined by the same grid.
caveats: Downtown/the Loop did not conform to the standard 800-per-mile grid until it was formally extended there on April 1, 1911 — pre-1909 addresses in the central area used a denser, inconsistent local numbering.

A handful of near-south-side streets deviate from the 800/mile rate: Roosevelt Rd (12th St) runs at 1,200 addresses/mile, Cermak Rd (22nd St) at 1,000/mile, and 31st St at 900/mile — an artifact of pre-1909 numbering that was never fully reconciled.

Diagonal streets (several following old Native American trails — Milwaukee Ave, Lincoln Ave, Ogden Ave, Elston Ave, Clybourn Ave, Archer Ave, Vincennes Ave, Clark St in parts) cut across the grid at an angle, so they don't carry a single fixed cross-grid number the way a true N-S or E-W street does, and their intersections with grid streets can be visually confusing.

Curving lakefront/river drives (Lake Shore Dr, Wacker Dr, Columbus Dr, Museum Campus Dr) don't hold a constant E/W or N/S position, so an address on them (e.g. Willis Tower's 233 S Wacker Dr) gives a reliable distance from Madison St but only an approximate east-west position — treat those as one-coordinate, not full-grid, addresses.

House numbers restart at the start of each new named street, and even-numbered addresses are conventionally on the north/west side of a street with odd numbers on the south/east side — useful for guessing which side of the street you want, but it's a convention, not a law with zero exceptions.

The system covers the City of Chicago and numbers carry into many (not all) adjoining suburbs that adopted the same baselines — a traveler crossing into a suburb with its own separate numbering system (e.g. Evanston, Oak Park in places) will see the grid logic stop applying cleanly.
